summary:
Kwara State stands under Nigeria's national framework: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA), signed in January 2014, applies nationwide, voids same-sex unions and criminalises forming, operating or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, with same-sex sexual activity carrying up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Kwara is not among the twelve states recorded as having adopted Sharia law (Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara), so no Sharia penal exposure is documented for the Ilorin area; the federal statute supplies the operative framework, with the Criminal Code operating in southern states and the Penal Code in northern states.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the SSMPA unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, though the core criminalisation provisions remain in force.

Human Rights Watch records that the SSMPA carries 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and bans same-sex cohabitation and public shows of same-sex amorous relationships. Its passage was followed by mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions of LGBT people across the country, including 21 young men arrested but never charged at an Ibadan birthday gathering. The report covers Nigeria nationally and names no Kwara-specific case; it documents the federal criminalisation and arbitrary enforcement that apply in Kwara.

Mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common across Nigeria, especially in northern states, per BBC News reporting of August 2024.
tangentialFactors: The killing of the 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as 'Abuja Area Mama', whose beaten body was found on a highway in Abuja in August 2024, illustrates the lethal violence facing trans Nigerians; she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life, and police opened an investigation. Her case occurred in Abuja, not Kwara, and is carried here as a national-pattern indicator rather than a Kwara incident.
localsOnly: No Kwara-specific enforcement incidents, arrests, or state-level legislative proposals were identified in the source inventory. The Human Rights Watch report names no Kwara-specific case.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 2022 ruling striking down Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the SSMPA has altered on-the-ground enforcement in Kwara is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Kwara-specific policing practice, venue closures, or extortion patterns are not documented in the inventory; the national pattern of mass arrests and 'looking gay' stops is carried by the parent record.
